### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

Chin and Chen give the field its first joint, quasi-experimental look at how Indiana's 2011 voucher-plus-charter-authorizer expansion affected district finances, operational inputs, local property-tax referenda, and district-level achievement, using a within-county difference-in-differences design with a baseline-predicted "choice exposure" index as treatment. The paper is unusually transparent — eleven specifications in Table 2, candid limitation-writing, and a self-reported conflicting study — and its best-supported findings can be relied on: districts predicted to be most exposed cut per-pupil expenditures (direction robust across every specification, magnitude somewhere between roughly \$160 and \$520 per pupil depending on the comparison group, and not significant once comparison districts are reweighted or bordering districts dropped), raised student-to-FTE-teacher ratios by about half a student, and held and passed more property-tax referenda, chiefly for capital projects. But the paper's most quotable claims are its least supported. The local-revenue mechanism that anchors the abstract's political-economy story is significant in only one of eleven specifications and positive in two; the claim that referenda "could not commensurately counteract" revenue losses is inferred from two separate models, never estimated; the achievement "reversal" rests on two pre-treatment years of district-mean SEDA data that cannot separate district effects from compositional change, and student-level Indiana work (Adger & Felegi 2024) finds the opposite sign; and the 2011 lapse of ARRA and levy-replacement funds — which fell hardest on exactly the larger, poorer districts the exposure index labels treated — is described in the paper's own context section but never tested as a confound. Read this as credible evidence on how Indiana's high-exposure districts adjusted spending and staffing after 2011 and as an agenda-setting first look at school choice and local tax politics; do not read it as settled evidence that choice reduces local revenues, weakens voter support for taxation, or lowers student achievement.

#### Key Strengths

- **A clean shock and a defensible dosage design.** Indiana's 2011 double reform has a single implementation date, so the staggered-DD pathologies genuinely do not apply, and the authors' elastic-net-predicted exposure index (built only from 2009-10 baseline covariates, jackknife-stable, with a first-stage in Appendix Figure A2) avoids defining treatment by post-policy uptake that is endogenous to district decisions.
- **Robustness reported with rare candor.** Table 2 prints eleven specifications — including the two (M10 inverse-propensity reweighting and M11 non-bordering comparisons) that attenuate the headline expenditure effect by 60-70% — and the text openly shows the estimated linear pre-trend flipping sign across 3-, 6-, and 9-year pre-windows. The county-by-year fixed effects and the honest disclosure of the effective sample (42 counties, 177 districts) are further marks of care.
- **A genuinely new outcome.** Hand-assembled, cross-verified Indiana referendum records brought into a causal design are without close precedent in the school-choice literature, and the capital-versus-operational split — exposed districts win levies for buildings but not for instruction — is a specific, policy-relevant fact that survives the demanding first-referendum-only restriction.
- **The whole causal chain in one setting.** Estimating finance, inputs, and achievement under one design and one treatment definition lets the paper speak to the Figure 1 mechanism chain rather than a single link, which few prior fiscal-spillover studies (Buerger & Bifulco, Mann & Bruno, Ridley & Terrier) manage.
- **Limitations stated, not performed.** The Conclusion names the SEDA composition problem, the rho ~ .75 correlation that prevents separating voucher from charter exposure, the mismatch between CES federal-spending items and local tax attitudes, and the cross-district enrollment problem, and it volunteers the contradicting Adger & Felegi (2024) result. The Indiana finance-context section is itself valuable institutional scholarship.

#### Key Concerns

- **An untested confound sits on top of the treatment definition.** Treated districts are, by construction, Indiana's larger, poorer, more urban, more heavily Black districts (Table 1: 6,513 vs. 2,096 students; \$979 vs. \$618 baseline federal revenue per pupil). ARRA funds and the 2008 circuit-breaker's levy-replacement grants both expired in 2011 on poverty- and tax-rate gradients that track that index; the federal-revenue decline in Panel E is exactly what a poverty-graded funding cliff produces. M6 (linear time trends by two demographic medians) is only a partial answer, and no honest-DD-style bound is reported.
- **The prose outruns Table 2.** The text calls results "generally robust in direction, magnitude, and statistical significance," but total expenditures fall from -\$521 (M4) to -\$201 and -\$161 (ns) in M10/M11; local revenue (Panel G) is significant only in the simple DD and positive in M2/M3; capital outlays are significant in one column; schools-in-operation in one. The Conclusion's "primarily driven by fewer dollars being received through local sources" is not what its own preferred specification shows.
- **The achievement result is the paper's most fragile and most citable claim.** Only two pre-treatment years exist, the post-period pattern is a monotone drift rather than a discrete reversal, district-mean SEDA scores confound district productivity with composition, the six subgroups are nested samples in the same districts, the largest negative estimates coincide with Indiana's 2015 and 2019 assessment transitions, and student-level work on the same reform finds improvement.
- **The referenda-versus-revenue "insufficiency" story is asserted, not estimated.** No exhibit puts levy dollars raised against appropriations lost. The +21pp/+12pp headline figures come from an "ever held / ever passed" DD that compares a ~2-year pre-window to an 8-year post-window and cannot show pre-trends; the paper's own event-study version gives +5pp (any) and +4pp (capital), and the stated-preference evidence that rescues the theory (CES, Appendix D) asks about Congress and represents state adults.
- **Reproducibility gaps and expository errors that readers will trip over.** No data availability statement, code, or software environment; unstated deflator and sample-inclusion rules; observation counts that do not follow from the stated panel; an Equation 4 time-centering contradiction (2011 vs. Year - 2012); a p. 17 significance claim contradicted by Figures 5 and 7; a broken abstract sentence; a Figure 2 with two contradictory legends; a "class size" label for a student-to-FTE ratio; and mangled reference entries (Jackson, Johnson & Persico; Ridley & Terrier; Friedman; Mann & Bruno's year).

#### What to Rely On

- Indiana districts with high predicted exposure to the 2011 choice expansion reduced per-pupil expenditures, particularly current (instructional) outlays, relative to low-exposure districts in the same county. The direction holds in all eleven specifications; treat the magnitude as a range (roughly -\$160 to -\$520 per pupil in the parametric models; up to ~\$680, or ~6.4% of baseline, at the 2019 endpoint of the event study) rather than a point.
- Student-to-FTE-teacher ratios rose in those districts by roughly half a student per teacher. The 2010-to-2012 jump is about ten times what the pre-trend slope predicts, and the effect survives the continuous-dose, IPW, and non-bordering checks (though it is borderline in M6-M8).
- High-exposure districts held and passed more property-tax referenda after 2011, and that effect is concentrated in capital rather than operational levies; the capital effect survives the first-referendum-only restriction (+11pp, significant) while the operational effect does not (+3pp).
- Predicted exposure to choice is a real dosage: the index predicts actual uptake only after 2011 (Appendix Figure A2), and 35% vs. 12% of public schools in treated vs. comparison districts sit within five miles of a charter or private school.
- The paper is the appropriate reference point for Indiana's 2011 voucher-plus-charter-authorizer bundle and for the argument that fiscal effects of choice are state-specific and must be estimated separately by finance system.
- The methodological point that a parametric linear event study would have masked the non-monotonic achievement pattern (and that pre-trend tests are window-dependent) is correct and well demonstrated.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- **"Revenue losses were primarily driven by local sources."** Local revenue (Table 2 Panel G) is significant only in the simple DD (M1), positive in M2 and M3, and -\$125.8 (SE 141.2) in the preferred M4; the Figure 7 pattern is partly the continuation of a large positive-to-zero pre-trend.
- **"Districts could not commensurately counteract shrinking revenues through referenda."** This is an inference across two separately estimated models; the paper never quantifies levy dollars raised against revenue lost, and the total-revenue estimate it depends on is itself window-dependent (ns in M3, significant in M4/M5).
- **"Short-term achievement gains reversed and became substantially negative."** Two pre-years, district-mean SEDA outcomes that mix district effects with composition, 90% intervals, a widest-interval 2019 endpoint that coincides with the ILEARN transition, and an opposite-signed student-level study (Adger & Felegi 2024) on the same reform.
- **"School choice weakens voter preferences for taxation."** The revealed-preference result points the other way (more referenda held and passed); the weakening-preferences reading rests on exploratory CES items about federal spending that the authors themselves say not to over-read.
- **Any statement about vouchers specifically.** The exposure index correlates .98 with predicted charter growth and .84 with predicted voucher uptake, so this is closer to charter-exposure evidence; the "conservative for vouchers" argument is theoretical, not tested.
- **The -2.4% housing-value mechanism, the 8/3/11pp first-referendum figures, and the school-proximity statistics.** All appear only in prose with no standard errors, sample sizes, or exhibits; the housing-value ACS-to-LEA geocoding is undescribed.
- **The p. 17 claim that pre-2011 coefficients "contain zero" and post-2011 coefficients "do not."** Figure 5's 2007 current-expenditure coefficient (+258) and Figure 7's 2006 revenue coefficients (+504, +521) have 90% CIs excluding zero; the paper's own p. 25 acknowledges a significant -\$45/year current-expenditure pre-trend.
- **The sample size.** Cite 177 districts (99 comparison, 78 treatment) in 42 counties — the effective sample disclosed on p. 31 — not the 287 in Table 1; and cite "class size" as a student-to-FTE-teacher ratio, which is what Figure 6 actually plots.
- **Generalization beyond Indiana.** The estimand is a within-county contrast between larger, poorer districts and their small rural neighbors under Indiana's circuit-breaker, referendum-gated finance system and its 2011 collective-bargaining restrictions (which removed class size from bargaining — the paper's clearest input margin). The authors flag this; readers in ESA/voucher-only states should not transport the estimates.

### Methods Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

This is a carefully executed, unusually transparent within-county difference-in-differences study that uses a machine-learning-predicted "choice exposure" index to define treated Indiana districts around the 2011 voucher/charter-authorizer reforms. The design is appropriate and the authors show their work — eleven specifications in Table 2, explicit discussion of pre-trend model dependence, spillover diagnostics, and a co-occurring-reform control — but the central magnitudes are more fragile than the narrative suggests, and treatment status is defined by district characteristics (poverty, urbanicity, Black enrollment share) that are also the incidence of the 2011 ARRA and levy-replacement funding cliffs, a confound the paper describes as context rather than tests as a threat.

**Strengths:**

- Treatment is defined by *predicted* rather than realized choice uptake, using a cross-validated elastic net over baseline (2009-10) SEDA and PSS covariates, which insulates group assignment from post-2011 district decisions that would be endogenous to the outcomes. The prediction model has adjusted R-squared of about .73, the selected predictors (share Black, share single mothers, private schools within 2 miles, baseline charter enrollment and count) are face-valid, and Note 4 reports a jackknife (leave-one-district-out) version that yields nearly identical treatment assignment. Appendix Figure A2 provides an explicit first-stage showing the index predicts realized choice uptake only after 2011.
- County-by-year fixed effects are a genuinely useful design choice: they absorb geographically local shocks (labor markets, county tax base, regional recovery from the Great Recession) that would otherwise contaminate a statewide pre/post comparison, and the authors report the resulting effective sample honestly (42 counties, 177 districts — 78 treated, 99 comparison — of the nominal 287; Appendix Table A3), rather than reporting the full-state N as if it identified the estimates.
- The robustness table is exceptionally candid about model dependence. Table 2 lays out the simple DD (M1), the parametric linear event study (M2-M3), three different pre-period windows (M3/M4/M5 = 6, 3, and 9 pre-years), controls for time trends interacted with the treatment-defining covariates (M6), a control for the co-occurring 2011 collective-bargaining reform (M7), an alternative first-post-year treatment definition (M8), a continuous ventile dose-response (M9), inverse-propensity reweighting of comparison districts (M10), and dropping comparison districts that border treated ones (M11). The authors explicitly show and discuss that the estimated linear pre-trend flips sign and significance across pre-period windows — a fragility most papers bury.
- The authors correctly reject the reflexive citation of staggered-DD literature: with one common treatment date and two groups, the Goodman-Bacon (2021) negative-weighting problem does not apply, and they say so rather than performing a decorative Callaway-Sant'Anna estimation.
- Prioritizing the nonparametric event study over the parametric linear version is the right call and is vindicated by the achievement results (Figure 9), where the post-period pattern is non-monotonic (early positive, later negative) and a linear post-trend specification would have averaged the two into near-zero. The paper makes this methodological point explicitly rather than letting the reader discover it.
- Serious multi-source data assembly: NCES district finance and CCD operational data, IDOE voucher counts assigned by students' LEA of legal settlement (so voucher exposure is measured without the cross-boundary ambiguity that afflicts charter measures), SEDA v5 achievement in NAEP-linked effect-size units by grade/subject/subgroup, PSS private-school proximity at four distance bands, referenda from IU CEEP cross-verified against Secretary of State election returns, plus ACS housing values and CES attitudes for mechanism probes. Achievement models are weighted by the number of assessments and include grade and subject fixed effects (Note 8).
- Spillover is addressed with actual evidence rather than assertion: geocoded pairwise school distances show 35% of treatment-district public schools versus 12% of comparison-district schools sit within 5 miles of a charter or private school in the same county, with mean nearest-alternative distances of 1.14 versus 3.28 miles — a defensible demonstration that the exposure index tracks real geographic dosage.

**Weaknesses:**

- The treatment index is nearly collinear with the incidence of two contemporaneous 2011 fiscal shocks that the paper itself describes but never treats as confounders. ARRA stimulus funds lapsed in 2011 and Indiana's levy replacement grants expired in 2011 — exactly the treatment date. ARRA was allocated largely through Title I/poverty channels, and Table 1 shows treated districts had baseline per-pupil federal revenue of \$979 versus \$618 in comparison districts and 3,450 versus 758 FRPL students. A district-poverty-graded federal funding cliff in 2011 mechanically produces the paper's federal revenue result (Panel E: -\$136.8 in M3, -\$140.5 in M5) and contributes to the total expenditure and revenue declines, with no voucher or charter involvement required. Similarly, the 2008 property-tax circuit breaker binds hardest in high-rate urban districts, which are disproportionately treated. M6 partially addresses this by interacting county-by-continuous-time with above/below-median Black share and single-mother share, but that is a linear time interaction on two dimensions only, not a flexible year-by-year control for baseline poverty or federal-aid dependence.
- The headline finance magnitudes do not survive the two comparison-group robustness checks. In Panel A, total per-pupil expenditures fall from -\$521.3 (M4, p<.01) to -\$201.1 (SE 131.2) under inverse-propensity reweighting (M10) and -\$161.1 (SE 163.8) when bordering comparison districts are dropped (M11) — a 60-70% attenuation in the point estimate, not merely a loss of precision. Current expenditures follow the same pattern (-\$322.5** in M4 versus -\$128.9 and -\$78.0). Capital outlays are significant only in M3 (-\$212.5**) and are -\$119.1 (ns) in the preferred M4 and +\$7.66 in M11. The text's summary that results are "generally robust in direction, magnitude, and statistical significance" is not an accurate description of Panels A-C in columns M10-M11.
- The paper's stated revenue mechanism — that declines are "primarily driven by fewer dollars being received through local sources" — is not supported by its own parametric table. Local revenue (Panel G) is statistically significant only in the simple DD of M1 (-\$297.1); it is +\$178.5 in M2, +\$72.29 in M3, -\$125.8 (SE 141.2, ns) in the preferred M4, -\$62.13 (ns) in M5, and -\$332.0 (SE 227.5, ns) in M11. Total revenue is likewise window-dependent: -\$141.6 (ns) with six pre-years (M3), -\$311.5** with three (M4), -\$380.6*** with nine (M5). Figure 7 shows why — the pre-period local and total revenue coefficients are large and positive (+\$504, +\$200, +\$199, +\$147) and decline monotonically toward the omitted 2011 baseline, so the "effect" is partly the continuation of a pre-existing convergence, and the answer depends entirely on how many pre-years the linear trend is fit to.
- Parallel trends is weakest exactly where the paper's causal story most needs it. Figure 6 shows a monotone class-size pre-trend (-0.59, -0.47, -0.34, -0.23, -0.22 from 2005 to 2010) and a monotone decline in schools in operation beginning well before 2011 (+0.023 down to -0.0075). Figure 7 shows a steep revenue pre-trend. And Figure 5's pre-period expenditure coefficients (e.g., -\$594, +\$208, +\$136) have 90% intervals spanning several hundred dollars, so "no significant pre-trend" reflects low power at least as much as it reflects parallel evolution. The paper does not report a formal sensitivity analysis in the Rambachan-Roth "honest DD" family, which is the standard tool for bounding results under exactly this kind of imperfect pre-trend; the linear-pre-trend adjustment in M4 is a reasonable substitute but, as the authors themselves demonstrate, is window-sensitive.
- Achievement is the most fragile outcome, not the most robust. Figure 9 has only two pre-treatment years (2009 and 2010), so the parallel-trends assumption is effectively untestable for this outcome, and the post-period pattern is a single monotone downward drift from +0.022 (2012) to -0.097 (2019). The authors concede that SEDA district means confound the district's contribution to learning with compositional change as students exit to charters and vouchers, and the subgroup breakdowns (White, male, female, economically disadvantaged, non-disadvantaged) are nested, overlapping samples within the same districts — their similarity is close to mechanical, not six independent confirmations. Adger and Felegi (2024), using student-level Indiana data, reach the opposite conclusion for voucher-exposed public schools.
- The exposure index measures charter exposure far more than voucher exposure. The paper reports that its overall predicted-exposure measure correlates about .98 with predicted charter enrollment growth and about .84 with predicted voucher uptake (and the two sector-specific predictions correlate about .75). A finding attributed to "school choice expansion" in a paper motivated substantially by Indiana's Choice Scholarship Program is therefore, empirically, closer to a charter-exposure contrast, and the authors' argument that pooling makes the estimates "conservative" with respect to a pure-voucher counterfactual is a theoretical conjecture, not evidence.
- The referenda analysis (Figure 8) uses a collapsed "ever held / ever passed" DD comparing a short pre-window (referenda in the sample begin only in 2009) to an eight-year post-window. "Ever" outcomes are concave in window length, so an asymmetric window can generate a positive DD from a constant underlying hazard gap. The paper's own event-study version, which can display pre-trends, yields a much more modest picture (about +5pp for any referendum, +4pp capital, per Appendix Table I1) than the +21pp / +22pp in Figure 8. Because passage is not conditioned on holding a referendum, the +12pp "passed any" coefficient mostly reflects that treated districts ask more often, not that voters became more willing when asked — and the paper's own first-referendum-only analysis attenuates results to +8pp (any), +3pp (operational), +11pp (capital), with only capital significant.
- Several smaller execution issues compound interpretation. All figures report 90% rather than 95% confidence intervals, so "significant" throughout the paper means p<.10. There is no adjustment for multiplicity across roughly nine outcomes, fourteen event-time coefficients, and six achievement subgroups. Finance regressions are unweighted, so estimates are district-averages even though treated districts are three times larger (6,513 versus 2,096 students), making the results a poor guide to how many students experienced the cuts. And every finance outcome is a per-pupil ratio whose denominator is itself treatment-affected — total-level expenditures and revenues are never shown, so a reader cannot tell whether treated districts cut spending faster than they lost students or merely differently.
- The political-economy channel — the paper's most novel theoretical contribution — rests on the thinnest evidence. The CES analysis in Appendix D asks respondents about what *Congress* should do on federal spending and taxation, is sampled to represent state adults rather than district residents, and is described by the authors themselves as imprecise and exploratory. The authors are appropriately hedged in the body text, but the abstract's framing around "voter tax preferences" rests mainly on the referenda results, which are the ones most affected by the window and conditioning issues above.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Treat the class-size result as the paper's most credible operational finding, but with a caveat. The jump from -0.22 students per FTE in 2010 to +0.62 in 2012 (Figure 6) is far larger than the ~0.075/year pre-trend would predict, and the effect survives the continuous-dose (M9: 0.0655***), IPW (M10: 0.468***), and no-bordering-comparison (M11: 0.551*) checks. Note, however, that it loses conventional significance in M6 (0.458, SE 0.278), M7 (0.461, SE 0.285), and M8 (0.456, SE 0.296) — so read it as "about half a student per teacher, robust in sign and rough magnitude, borderline once baseline-demographic time trends are absorbed."
- Read the headline expenditure number as an upper bound, not a point estimate. The abstract's claim that treated districts "decreased expenditures" is directionally well supported across M1-M9, but the credible range is roughly -\$160 to -\$520 per pupil rather than the -\$600 to -\$700 suggested by Figure 5's largest event-study coefficients. If you need a single figure for policy arithmetic, use M10/M11's attenuated estimates as the conservative anchor and state that the finding is not significant once comparison districts are reweighted to match pre-policy levels.
- Do not cite this paper for the claim that school choice reduces *local* revenue specifically. Panel G of Table 2 is significant in only one of eleven specifications (the simple DD, M1) and is positive in two others (M2, M3). The narrative that "the largest drop in absolute terms can be seen in local revenues" comes from the nonparametric event study levels (Figure 7), which do not adjust for the clear positive-to-negative pre-trend visible in that same panel.
- Before building on the finance results, satisfy yourself that the 2011 ARRA and levy-replacement expirations are not doing the work. Both lapsed in the treatment year, both were allocated in ways correlated with district poverty, and treated districts had 58% higher baseline per-pupil federal revenue. The federal-revenue decline (Panel E) is exactly what a poverty-graded stimulus cliff produces. A reader who wants to rely on the expenditure result should check whether it survives controlling flexibly for baseline federal revenue share or ARRA receipt interacted with year — a test the paper does not report.
- Treat the achievement "reversal" (Figure 9) as the paper's most speculative claim. With only two pre-treatment years, parallel trends is untestable for this outcome; the estimates are 90% intervals; the pattern is a single monotone drift rather than a discrete reversal; and district-mean SEDA scores confound district value-added with compositional change as students exit. The largest negative estimates (2018: -0.076; 2019: -0.097) also coincide with Indiana's assessment transitions (the 2015 ISTEP+ redesign and the 2019 shift to ILEARN); SEDA's NAEP linking and the county-by-year fixed effects absorb statewide shocks but not test-transition effects that vary with district composition. Note also that Adger and Felegi (2024), using student-level data, find the opposite sign for voucher-exposed public schools.
- Anchor referenda claims on the event-study estimates in Appendix I, not on Figure 8's +21pp / +22pp. The "ever held / ever passed" construction compares roughly two pre-years to eight post-years, which mechanically inflates an "ever" contrast. And because passage is not conditioned on holding a referendum, the +12pp passage coefficient is not evidence that voters became more supportive — the operational-referendum passage effect (+5.3pp) is not significant, and the first-referendum-only analysis leaves only capital referenda significant.
- Interpret "school choice exposure" here as predominantly charter exposure. Given the .98 correlation between the exposure index and predicted charter enrollment versus .84 for voucher uptake, this paper is weaker evidence about voucher effects specifically than its framing implies — a relevant caution given that the current policy debate is about universal ESA/voucher programs, not charter authorizer counts.
- Note what the estimand actually is. County-by-year fixed effects mean identification comes only from the 42 counties containing both high- and low-predicted-exposure districts (177 of 287 districts). Treated districts are, by construction of the elastic net, larger, poorer, more urban, and more heavily Black-enrolled; comparison districts are small rural districts in the same county. The result is "how urban/higher-poverty districts fared relative to their small rural county neighbors after 2011," which is a within-county contrast, not a state-average policy effect, and is not directly transportable to states without Indiana's post-2008 circuit-breaker finance system or its 2011 collective-bargaining restrictions (which barred class-size bargaining — the very margin on which the paper finds its clearest input effect).
- Do not cite the CES results as causal evidence that school choice reduces support for taxation. They ask about federal spending and Congress, represent state adults rather than district residents, and the authors themselves flag imprecision and missingness. The housing-value analysis (-2.4% median home value from the ACS DD) is a more concrete mechanism candidate for the local-revenue story, but it too is a single unreplicated DD estimate.
- When reading the confidence intervals, remember that all figures use 90% bars and that no multiplicity adjustment is applied across roughly nine outcomes, fourteen event-time coefficients, and six achievement subgroups. The six achievement subgroups are nested, overlapping samples in the same districts, so their "strikingly similar" patterns are close to mechanical and should not be read as six independent replications.

**Detailed Commentary:**

The core design is well matched to the question. Indiana's May 2011 double reform — the Choice Scholarship voucher program plus expansion of charter authorizers beyond Ball State and the Indianapolis mayor — is a genuine statewide shock with a single, clean implementation date, which is why the authors can legitimately set aside the staggered-adoption DD literature (Goodman-Bacon 2021). Since every district in the state is nominally exposed, the identification problem is not treated-versus-untreated but dosage, and the authors' solution — a cross-validated elastic net predicting post-period charter-plus-voucher uptake from 2009-10 SEDA and PSS covariates, then trichotomized with the top tercile as treated — is a defensible approach in the Jackson-Johnson-Persico tradition. Using predicted rather than realized uptake is the right instinct, because realized uptake responds to the very district decisions (school closures, program cuts) that are the outcomes of interest. The jackknife check in Note 4 and the first-stage in Appendix Figure A2 are the right supporting diagnostics.

But a predicted-exposure index built from baseline covariates is, mechanically, just a weighted index of baseline district characteristics — here dominated by share Black, share single mothers, private-school proximity, and baseline charter presence. Table 1 makes the consequence vivid: treated districts enroll 6,513 students on average versus 2,096, serve 3,450 FRPL students versus 758, are 11% Black versus 0.5%, and receive \$979 in per-pupil federal revenue versus \$618. So the DD contrast is "larger, poorer, more urban districts versus their small rural county neighbors, before versus after 2011." County-by-year fixed effects handle geography but not district type, and the design's internal validity therefore turns entirely on whether anything else in 2011 hit larger, poorer districts differentially. Something did — two things, in fact, and the paper describes both in its own context section without treating them as threats. ARRA stimulus appropriations lapsed in 2011, and Indiana's levy replacement grants (the transitional support for the 2008 circuit-breaker property-tax overhaul) expired in 2011. Both were allocated on poverty and property-tax-rate gradients that align closely with the treatment index. The federal revenue findings in Panel E of Table 2 (-\$136.8 in M3, -\$140.5 in M5) are precisely what a poverty-graded federal funding cliff produces with no charter or voucher involvement whatsoever, and the total expenditure declines partly inherit that. The M6 specification — county-by-continuous-time interacted with above/below-median Black share and single-mother share — is the closest the paper comes to testing this, but it is a linear time interaction on two dimensions, not a flexible year-by-year absorption of baseline poverty or stimulus dependence. A reader should regard this as the largest unaddressed identification threat in the paper.

The second thing to know is that the paper's own Table 2 is more equivocal than its prose. The transparency here is admirable — most papers would not print M10 and M11 — but the summary sentence that findings are "generally robust in direction, magnitude, and statistical significance" does not describe what those columns show. Total per-pupil expenditures go from -\$521.3 (SE 187.2, p<.01) in the preferred M4 to -\$201.1 (SE 131.2) under inverse-propensity reweighting and -\$161.1 (SE 163.8) when bordering comparison districts are excluded. Because the point estimates fall by 60-70%, this is not simply a power loss from the smaller M11 sample (1,649 observations). Capital outlays are significant in exactly one column (M3, -\$212.5) and are near zero in M11. Most consequentially for the paper's narrative, the local revenue channel — which the abstract and conclusion identify as the primary driver of revenue losses — is statistically significant in only the simple DD of M1 (-\$297.1), and is positive in M2 (+\$178.5) and M3 (+\$72.29). Total revenue is significant in M4 and M5 but not M3, and the difference is purely the number of pre-years used to fit the linear trend. The authors say so explicitly and defend M4 by analogy to local-linear estimation in RD, which is a reasonable argument, but the reader should register that the revenue result is a specification choice as much as a finding.

The pre-trend evidence deserves closer reading than "no significant pre-trends" suggests. In Figure 7, the pre-period revenue coefficients are +\$504, +\$200, +\$199, and +\$147, declining monotonically toward the omitted 2011 baseline — a downward drift of roughly \$100 per year that, extrapolated, would generate most or all of the post-2011 declines without any policy at all. In Figure 6, class size trends monotonically upward from -0.59 to -0.22 and schools in operation trend monotonically downward from +0.023 to -0.0075, both starting years before treatment. Figure 5's expenditure pre-period coefficients are individually insignificant but with 90% intervals spanning hundreds of dollars, so the non-rejection is a statement about power, not about parallel evolution. This is exactly the setting the Rambachan-Roth honest-DD framework was designed for — bounding treatment effects under smooth violations of parallel trends calibrated to the observed pre-period — and its absence is the most material methodological gap. The authors' parametric linear-pre-trend correction (M4) is a serviceable substitute, and to their credit they demonstrate its own instability across pre-period windows, but the reader is left without a principled bound. The one place where the pre-trend concern is clearly answered is class size: the 2010-to-2012 jump of +0.84 is roughly ten times what the pre-trend slope predicts over two years, so that discontinuity is real even if its precise magnitude is uncertain.

The achievement analysis is the weakest link and should be read with the most caution, despite being the finding most likely to be cited. There are only two pre-treatment years (2009 and 2010) because SEDA coverage begins then, which means the parallel-trends assumption is essentially untestable for this outcome. The post-period pattern is a single monotone drift from +0.022 in 2012 to -0.097 in 2019, not a genuine reversal around an identifiable inflection; the same series with two more pre-years might well look like a continuing downward trajectory. The authors are commendably explicit that district-mean SEDA scores confound the district's own contribution to learning with compositional change as students exit to vouchers and charters, and their subgroup analysis only partially addresses this, because within-subgroup selection is still free to move. The six subgroups are nested, overlapping samples drawn from the same districts, so the fact that they look alike is close to arithmetic rather than six independent replications. Two further wrinkles: Indiana redesigned ISTEP+ in 2015 and replaced it with ILEARN in spring 2019 — the year of the largest negative estimate — and while SEDA's NAEP linking and the county-by-year fixed effects absorb statewide shocks, they do not absorb transition effects that vary with district composition. And Adger and Felegi (2024), whom the authors cite fairly, find the opposite sign for voucher-exposed Indiana public schools using student-level data. The finding is interesting and worth taking seriously as a hypothesis; it is not settled.

The referenda analysis has a specific construction problem worth flagging. Figure 8 collapses time and asks whether a district ever held or ever passed a referendum in the pre- versus post-period, but referenda in the sample only begin in 2009, so a roughly two-year pre-window is being compared to an eight-year post-window. "Ever" outcomes are concave in window length, so an asymmetric window can produce a positive DD even under a constant treatment-comparison hazard gap. The authors' motivation for collapsing (fewer than 10%, often fewer than 5%, of districts hold a vote in any given year) is sound on power grounds, but the tradeoff is that they cannot show pre-trends for the headline specification. Their own year-by-year event-study version in Appendix I yields a much more modest picture (+5pp for any referendum, +4pp for capital) than Figure 8's +21pp and +22pp. Because passage is not conditioned on holding a referendum, the +12pp "passed any" coefficient largely reflects the increased propensity to ask; the operational-referendum passage effect (+5.3pp) is not significant, and the first-referendum-only analysis leaves only capital referenda significant (+11pp). The honest summary of the referenda evidence is: treated districts asked more often, chiefly for capital projects, and got those capital asks approved; there is no reliable evidence that voters became more willing to fund day-to-day operations, which is where the instructional money is.

Some smaller matters that nonetheless affect how estimates should be read. All figures use 90% confidence intervals, so every claim of significance in the graphical results is at p<.10. No multiplicity adjustment is applied across roughly nine outcomes, fourteen event-time coefficients, and six subgroups. Finance regressions are unweighted, so a treated district of 25,000 students and one of 1,500 count equally; because treated districts are three times larger on average, the district-level estimates are not a good guide to how many students actually experienced the cuts. Every finance outcome is a per-pupil ratio whose denominator responds to treatment; total-level expenditures and revenues are never reported, so a reader cannot decompose whether treated districts cut faster or slower than they lost enrollment — which is the theoretically pivotal question the paper's own economies-of-scale framework raises in the Theoretical Frameworks section. Clustering at the district level is the right choice given treatment is district-level and time-invariant, though with 78 treated clusters in the estimation sample, and binary rare outcomes for referenda, the asymptotics are not comfortable. Finally, the M9 continuous ventile specification is subject to the continuous-treatment DD concerns in the de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille line of work, which the paper's dismissal of "recent advances" on single-treatment-period grounds does not cover.

One framing point that matters for citation practice: the paper's exposure index correlates about .98 with predicted charter enrollment growth and about .84 with predicted voucher uptake, and the two sector-specific predictions correlate about .75 with each other. The paper is therefore weaker evidence about vouchers specifically than its motivation (Indiana's Choice Scholarship, second-largest voucher program in the country) implies. The authors acknowledge this and argue the pooling makes estimates conservative relative to a pure-voucher counterfactual, but that argument is theoretical — derived from Pierson's incentive-effects logic — not empirical. Given that the live national policy debate is about universal ESA and voucher expansion rather than charter authorizer counts, readers should be careful not to transport these results to voucher-only settings.

On balance: this is competent, honest, well-documented quasi-experimental work that assembles an impressive multi-source dataset and reports its own fragility more openly than most published DD papers. It is not a paper whose central estimates should be treated as settled magnitudes. The load-bearing conclusions are (1) that high-choice-exposure Indiana districts increased class sizes by roughly half a student per FTE, which survives most but not all checks, and (2) that per-pupil expenditures declined in those districts, directionally robust but with a credible range that reaches down toward statistical insignificance under two of the eleven specifications. The local-revenue mechanism, the capital-expenditure effect, the school-closure result (significant only in M1), the achievement reversal, and the voter-preference channel are all more contingent than the abstract conveys, and each rests on a specific analytic choice a skeptical reader would want to interrogate before building on it.

### Literature Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

Chin and Chen assemble a compact (~46-reference), well-organized, and mostly honest account of the charter-fiscal-spillover literature and pair it with a genuinely useful political-science framing (Pierson's policy feedback, Mettler's submerged state, Labaree/Lubienski on public vs. private purposes) that is rare in school-finance work. But the review is thin for AERJ on three fronts that bear directly on the headline claims: the voucher-specific competitive- and fiscal-effects literature, Indiana-specific school-choice research, and the public-finance/referenda/Tiebout tradition in which the paper's novel "voter tax preferences" contribution actually sits. Several novelty claims — especially about causal evidence on individuals' attitudes — outrun what the cited literature and the paper's own design support, and a handful of reference-list errors mean specific citations should be verified before repeating.

**Strengths:**

- The core charter fiscal-spillover literature is covered competently and with the right studies: Arsen & Ni (2012), Bifulco & Reback (2014), Buerger & Bifulco (2019), Cook (2018), Ladd & Singleton (2020), Mann & Bruno (2022), and Ridley & Terrier (2025). These are the appropriate antecedents, and the paper is honest that this evidence base is genuinely mixed rather than cherry-picking a direction.
- The theoretical framing is the paper's strongest scholarly move. Bringing Pierson's (1993) incentive vs. interpretive policy-feedback distinction and Mettler's (2011) submerged state to bear on school finance is a real cross-disciplinary contribution, and the incentive/interpretive split does useful analytic work later (it is what lets the authors reason about why charters and vouchers might differ in their downstream effects on tax support).
- The paper engages both quantitative and qualitative/critical traditions rather than dismissing one. Castillo (2020), Hernández & Castillo (2022), Wells et al. (2002), Singer & Lenhoff (2022), Ewing (2018), and Shaw (2017) sit alongside the econometric work, and the qualitative citations are used substantively (to motivate mechanisms about leader responses and about who cannot exit) rather than decoratively.
- The authors surface the most damaging piece of conflicting evidence themselves. Adger and Felegi (2024) find that Indiana public schools most exposed to voucher growth improved, which cuts directly against this paper's negative long-run achievement result, and Chin and Chen state it plainly and offer a reasoned account of the difference (district-level SEDA aggregates vs. student-level data; charter-plus-voucher scope vs. voucher-only).
- The Indiana policy-context section (2008 circuit breaker, the shift from local levies to state sales tax, complexity funding, ARRA expiration, the 2011 levy-replacement grant sunset) is unusually careful institutional scholarship and is essential to reading the results correctly — it is arguably the most valuable part of the paper for readers who work on state school-finance systems.

**Weaknesses:**

- The voucher-specific empirical literature is largely absent, even though a voucher program is half the treatment. The canonical causal studies of how means-tested vouchers affect students remaining in public schools — Figlio & Hart (2014, AEJ: Applied) and Figlio, Hart & Karbownik (on scaling up Florida's program) on Florida, and Chakrabarti (2008, J. Public Economics) on Milwaukee — are not cited. These generally find null-to-positive competitive effects on public school achievement, which is the most direct conflicting evidence for this paper's negative long-run achievement finding, and it goes unaddressed.
- Indiana-specific school-choice research is nearly missing. Waddington & Berends (2018, JPAM) on the achievement effects of the Indiana Choice Scholarship Program, and the broader Notre Dame program of research on Indiana's choice landscape (Berends, Waddington, and colleagues), are the obvious antecedents for a paper built entirely on Indiana's 2011 reforms. The only Indiana antecedent cited is Adger and Felegi (2024), an unpublished SSRN working paper. Readers should not take this paper's framing as an accurate map of what is already known about Indiana.
- The literature underpinning the paper's self-described novel contribution — voter tax preferences — is the thinnest part of the main text. Tiebout (1956) is never cited despite a sorting-and-capitalization argument running through the theory section and the conclusion's housing-value mechanism. The school-bond/referendum literature in economics (Cellini, Ferreira & Rothstein 2010 on bond RDs), the political economy of who supports school spending (Poterba 1997 on demographic structure; Alesina, Baqir & Easterly 1999 on heterogeneity and public goods), and the capitalization literature beyond Brehm et al. (Black 1999; Bayer, Ferreira & McMillan 2007) are all absent from the main text. Note the mitigating fact: Note 1 says online Appendix F summarizes work on the predictors of school funding referenda, so some of this may be there — but relegating the foundational literature for the paper's headline novelty to an appendix leaves the main-text framing weaker than it should be.
- Novelty on attitudes is oversold. The paper claims to provide "plausibly causal evidence on how school choice specifically affects individuals' attitudes toward government taxation and spending." What is actually estimated causally is district-level referendum behavior (whether one is held and whether it passes) — an institutional decision plus an aggregate vote, not an individual attitude. The genuine attitudinal analysis (Cooperative Election Study) is in an appendix, uses questions about federal spending, and the authors themselves caution against overinterpretation. Casalaspi (2019) had already studied choice exposure and school bond elections in Michigan, so the marginal novelty is narrower than "hardly any studies explore" implies.
- The achievement literature is handled almost entirely through three review articles (Cohodes & Parham 2021; Egalite & Wolf 2016; Jabbar et al. 2022) rather than primary studies. That is efficient framing, but it means the paper's own negative achievement estimate is never placed against specific competitive-effects estimates (e.g., Imberman 2011; Cordes 2018; Winters 2012 on charter competition; the Florida voucher work above), and readers get no sense of where this estimate falls in that distribution.
- Both proposed mechanisms are under-cited relative to how much interpretive weight they carry. School closures are supported by Ewing (2018) and Shaw (2017) — valuable ethnographic and legal work, but the quantitative closure literature (e.g., Engberg, Gill, Zamarro & Zimmer 2012; Brummet 2014) is absent. Class size rests on Chetty et al. (2011) from Project STAR, where the treatment was a reduction of roughly seven students; this paper's estimated increase is 0.5 to 0.75 students. The scale mismatch between the cited evidence and the estimated mechanism is never discussed.
- Reference-list errors that readers will trip over. Jackson, Johnson & Persico (2016) is listed as "Quarterly Journal of Economics, 157, 218" (the volume and pages are mangled; it is QJE 131(1), 157-218). Mann & Bruno is cited as 2020 in the introduction but 2022 elsewhere, and only 2022 appears in the reference list. Friedman (1955) has no source at all. Ridley & Terrier's page range ("1356-140") is malformed. Also, the sentence characterizing Fleming (2014) — "voucher parents were more likely to see the government's role in education policy" — is incoherent as printed and appears to be missing a word or negation; Fleming's Milwaukee finding is generally read as voucher parents being less supportive of government provision and taxation for public schools.
- Two factual claims in the framing carry no citation and have likely aged: that Indiana's program is "second in the country in absolute size only to Ohio's EdChoice program (88,000)" — this depends entirely on an unstated year and is not obviously true once Florida's and Arizona's ESA expansions are counted — and that "more than 30% of families" use school choice, attributed to Wang et al. (2019), an NCES report whose definition of choice includes chosen public schools, private schools, and homeschooling. Both numbers are quotable and both need their definitions checked before being repeated.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Before treating this paper as evidence that school choice depresses public school achievement, read it alongside Figlio & Hart (2014, AEJ: Applied) on Florida's tax-credit scholarship, Figlio, Hart & Karbownik on the scaled-up Florida program, and Chakrabarti (2008, J. Public Economics) on Milwaukee. Those studies use arguably cleaner competition measures and find null-to-positive effects on students remaining in public schools. This paper does not engage them, so the reader must do the reconciling.
- Read Adger and Felegi (2024) directly rather than through this paper's summary. It is the closest Indiana antecedent, uses student-level rather than district-aggregate data, and reaches the opposite achievement conclusion. Chin and Chen's explanation (composition vs. contribution; charters plus vouchers vs. vouchers alone) is plausible but is offered in a late conclusion paragraph, not tested. Which study you believe should turn on how much you trust SEDA district aggregates to separate compositional change from district productivity — a limitation the authors concede.
- For Indiana context the paper does not supply, go to Waddington & Berends (2018, JPAM) on the Choice Scholarship Program's achievement effects and the wider Notre Dame research program on Indiana school choice (Berends, Waddington, and colleagues). Anyone citing this paper as "the" Indiana school-choice evidence would be misrepresenting the field.
- Situate the tax-preference contribution against the public-finance literature the paper does not cite in the main text: Tiebout (1956) for the sorting logic; Cellini, Ferreira & Rothstein (2010, QJE) for credible identification off bond referenda; Poterba (1997) and Alesina, Baqir & Easterly (1999) for who supports public education spending and why; Brunner and Sonstelie's work on homeowners, property values, and voter support for California's voucher initiative, which is a close conceptual antecedent for the choice-to-tax-preferences link. Check online Appendix F first — the authors say some referendum-predictor literature lives there.
- Cite this paper for the district-level fiscal and referendum results in Indiana, not for causal evidence on individual attitudes. The referendum outcomes are the estimated objects; the attitudinal claim rests on exploratory Cooperative Election Study analysis about federal spending that the authors themselves say should not be over-read. On the political-participation side, Cook, Kogan, Lavertu & Peskowitz (2020) and Casalaspi (2019) remain the primary sources, and this paper extends rather than supersedes them.
- Note the direction of the referendum finding before repeating the paper's framing. The theory in Figure 1 predicts weakening support for taxing to fund public schools; the revealed-preference results show treated districts are more likely to hold and to pass referenda, driven by capital rather than operating levies. The authors reinterpret this as insufficient rather than contradictory, and offer a district-effort explanation. That reinterpretation is reasonable but is a judgment call, and readers who accept the abstract's phrasing without reading the results section will miss it.
- Verify four citations before reusing them: Jackson, Johnson & Persico (2016) — the volume and pages in the reference list are wrong (QJE 131(1), 157-218); Mann & Bruno — the introduction says 2020, the list says 2022; Friedman (1955) — no publication source is given (it appeared in Solo's *Economics and the Public Interest*); and the Fleming (2014) characterization, which is garbled as printed and should be read in the original.
- For the mechanisms, supplement rather than rely on the paper. On closures, the quantitative literature (Engberg, Gill, Zamarro & Zimmer 2012; Brummet 2014) gives magnitudes that Ewing (2018) and Shaw (2017), valuable as they are, do not. On class size, benchmark the estimated 0.5-to-0.75-student increase against the roughly seven-student STAR reduction behind Chetty et al. (2011) before accepting class size as a sufficient channel for the achievement decline.
- For a fuller picture of the charter fiscal literature, add Epple, Romano & Zimmer's survey of charter school research, Ladd's (2019, JPAM) argument on charters and the public interest, and the Michigan district fiscal-stress work by Arsen and colleagues, which is the closest existing treatment of the "enrollment death spiral" the paper theorizes about but does not test.

**Detailed Commentary:**

Where this paper actually sits in the field. The paper claims three contributions, and they carry very different weights. The fiscal-spillover contribution is real but incremental: Ridley & Terrier (2025) do essentially this design in Massachusetts, Buerger & Bifulco (2019) in New York, Ladd & Singleton (2020) in North Carolina, and Cook (2018) on unionized districts. Chin and Chen's honest framing — that heterogeneity across state finance systems is expected and that the field should accumulate state-specific estimates — is the right way to describe this, and the paper should be cited that way: as the Indiana entry in a growing series, notable because Indiana bundles a large voucher program with charter expansion under a circuit-breaker-constrained local levy system. The achievement contribution is the weakest, both because SEDA district aggregates cannot separate compositional change from district productivity (the authors concede this) and because the paper does not engage the primary competitive-effects studies that point the other way. The tax-preference contribution is the most interesting and the most oversold; see below.

The voucher gap. This is the omission that matters most. Every fiscal-spillover study the paper cites is about charter schools. Charters and vouchers differ in ways that are central to the paper's own theory — the incentive/interpretive distinction the authors borrow from Pierson turns precisely on whether the exiting family remains inside the public system — and the authors say as much in the conclusion when reasoning about why voucher-driven exposure might produce larger effects. Yet the empirical literature on how voucher programs affect the districts and students left behind (Figlio & Hart on Florida; Chakrabarti on Milwaukee; the Figlio-Hart-Karbownik scaling-up work) is entirely absent, and so is the fiscal-impact literature on voucher programs specifically. The consequence for readers is asymmetric: the missing achievement work mostly runs against this paper's negative finding, so its absence makes the paper's result look less contested than it is.

The attitudes claim, precisely. The paper says its contribution is "plausibly causal evidence on how school choice specifically affects individuals' attitudes toward government taxation and spending," and frames Fleming (2014) as limited because it "required strong assumptions for causality." But the causally identified outcome here is whether a district holds a referendum and whether it passes — a variable that mixes district leadership strategy (the authors acknowledge treated districts may "invest more effort in the referenda process"), voter turnout composition, and voter preferences, and which cannot be decomposed into those parts with the data at hand. The actual attitudinal measure, from the Cooperative Election Study, is in an appendix, asks about congressional spending rather than local levies, is described as exploratory and imprecise, and is used to make district-level inferences from a sample that at best represents state adults. Both statements can be true: the referendum results are a valuable revealed-preference contribution, and the individual-attitudes framing is not supported. Readers who cite the paper for the second claim will be over-claiming on the authors' behalf.

The internal tension readers should notice. Figure 1's theory predicts that choice expansion erodes support for taxing to fund public schools. The estimated referendum effects go the other way — up to 21 percentage points more likely to hold a vote, 12 points more likely to hold and pass one. The authors handle this in three moves: the effects are concentrated in capital rather than operating referenda; effects attenuate when restricted to each district's first post-2011 referendum; and passing levies may still fail to offset revenue declines. Each move is defensible, and the capital-versus-operating distinction is a genuinely useful finding. But the cumulative effect is that the paper's cleanest positive result is reinterpreted as consistent with a theory predicting the opposite sign. This is the place where an unengaged literature would have helped most: the school-bond and levy-election literature in economics and political science has a well-developed account of why capital and operating measures behave differently (capital levies are salient, bounded, and tied to visible assets; operating levies are recurring and diffuse), and drawing on it would have made the interpretation an argument rather than a reconciliation.

Adjacent-field placement. The political science borrowing is the paper's distinctive scholarly move and is well executed at the theory level — Pierson and Mettler are used correctly and non-decoratively. The weakness is that the empirical political-science literature is engaged through a single review (Larsen 2019) plus four specific studies, which is a thin basis for the claim that political scientists' education work "does not necessarily investigate school choice per se or outcomes beyond civic participation." The public-economics side is where placement is weakest: a paper whose causal chain runs choice, then property values, then local revenue, then referenda ought to be in conversation with Tiebout, the capitalization literature beyond Brehm et al. (2017), and the political economy of local public-goods provision. The 2.4 percent median housing-value decline reported in the conclusion is presented as a mechanism with essentially no literature attached to it, despite being the load-bearing explanation for why per-pupil local revenues fall when Indiana's formula loses districts a flat per-student amount.

Sociology and qualitative traditions. Coverage here is better than in most quantitative school-finance papers. Labaree (1997) and Lubienski (2003) are used to motivate the interpretive-effects channel, Wells et al. (2002) for the neoliberal-policy framing, and Singer & Lenhoff (2022) for the equity implication that families with weaker alternatives cannot exit. What is missing is the qualitative literature on how district and school leaders actually respond to competition — Jabbar's New Orleans work is the obvious example, and Jabbar appears only as a coauthor on the 2022 systematic review. That literature speaks directly to the paper's central mechanism claim that leaders' perceptions of competition may matter as much as realized enrollment loss, which the paper asserts theoretically and never evidences.

Limits of this assessment. I did not read the online supplementary appendices, and Note 1 indicates Appendix F contains additional literature on tax attitudes and on the predictors of school-funding referenda. If that appendix is substantial, my criticism of the referendum-literature gap should be read as a criticism of main-text framing rather than of scholarship. I also cannot verify the accuracy of every characterization against the primary sources; the ones I flag as garbled (Fleming) or malformed (the Jackson, Johnson & Persico reference; the Mann & Bruno year; the Ridley & Terrier pages; the incomplete Friedman entry) are detectable from the paper's own text. My knowledge of the charter fiscal-spillover and voucher competitive-effects literatures is good; my knowledge of the Indiana-specific policy-analysis literature and of the referendum-determinants literature is less complete, so there may be additional Indiana work I have not named.

---

### Writing Review

**Rating:** Adequate (high confidence)

The paper is well-organized, readable, and unusually transparent about its own robustness checks and limitations, with clearly numbered research questions that map one-to-one onto results subsections. But the exposition repeatedly runs ahead of the exhibits: a categorical claim about statistical significance in the Results is contradicted by the paper's own Figures 5 and 7 and by its own later text; the headline mechanism (revenue losses "primarily driven by" local sources) is significant in only one of eleven specifications in Table 2; the abstract contains a broken key sentence and omits the finding that referenda actually increased; and Figure 2 carries two mutually contradictory legends plus a series the text promises but that is not plotted. Readers can trust the direction of the expenditure and achievement findings but should verify every quantitative claim against the figures before quoting it.

**Strengths:**

- Exceptionally clear architecture: five numbered RQs stated on pp. 2-3, four "main findings" previewed in the introduction, and Results subsections that follow the RQ order exactly. A reader can navigate to any answer in seconds.
- Robustness discussion is interleaved with results rather than exiled to an appendix ("Robustness of School Finance and Operations Results" sits between the revenue and referenda sections). This is reader-friendly: the credibility assessment arrives while the estimate is still in mind.
- The methods exposition is genuinely instructive. The elastic-net treatment-assignment procedure (Eqs. 2-3) is explained in plain language including the motivation (avoiding researcher degrees of freedom), the selected predictors, and a face-validity argument. The parametric-vs-nonparametric event-study tradeoff (pp. 25-26) is one of the clearest short treatments of that choice in the education-policy literature, and the authors explicitly note that a linear specification would have masked the nonlinear achievement pattern.
- The Indiana context section (pp. 8-11) gives readers the institutional detail they need to interpret the estimates: the 2008 circuit-breaker legislation, the shift from local to state funding, complexity dollars, and the referendum requirement.
- The Conclusion is candid and specific about limitations rather than performative: CES respondents are asked about Congress not local government; SEDA data cannot follow individual students so composition shifts are conflated with district effects; voucher and charter exposure predictions correlate at rho ~ .75 so the two policies cannot be separated; cross-district choice may misassign exposure. The authors also volunteer a contrary finding (Adger & Felegi, 2024, who find positive effects using student-level data).
- Figure 1's schema, referenced again in the Conclusion, gives the paper a spine, and the note distinguishing solid-arrow (tested) from other relationships is a good self-containment practice.

**Weaknesses:**

- A categorical significance claim is false on the paper's own figures. On p. 17 the text states that "the 90% confidence intervals for estimated gamma-T coefficients after 2011 do not contain zero" and that "across finance outcomes, treatment-comparison differences are significant only after 2011, and no clear differential pre-trend emerges (i.e., estimated gamma-T coefficients before 2011 contain zero)." In Figure 5, the 2007 current-expenditures coefficient (+258) has a 90% CI that clearly excludes zero, and the 2012 total-expenditures coefficient (-178) has a CI that appears to include zero. In Figure 7, the 2006 coefficients for total revenue (+504) and local revenue (+521) both have CIs excluding zero. The paper itself later contradicts the claim on p. 25, noting the significant -44.59 per-year pre-trend for current expenditures "observed visually in the associated ES figure (Figure 5)."
- The "local revenues" mechanism, which anchors the abstract's political-economy story and the housing-value explanation on p. 33, is the least robust result in the paper. In Table 2 Panel G, the local-revenue coefficient is significant only in M1 (the simple DD, -297.1***). In every other specification (M2-M11) it is insignificant, and in M2/M3 it is positive (+178.5, +72.29). The preferred M4 gives -125.8 (141.2). The Results section hedges appropriately ("not consistently significant... when disentangled"), but the Conclusion drops the hedge ("primarily driven by fewer dollars being received through local sources") and the abstract's framing depends on it.
- Abstract fidelity problems. (a) The second sentence is grammatically broken and arguably says the opposite of what is meant: "little rigorous work confirms the conceptual link between privatization and increased competition in K-12 education with enthusiasm for public goods and the tax policies they require" — the word "decreased" appears to have been lost before "enthusiasm." (b) "could not commensurately counteract shrinking revenues through local property tax referenda" omits the paper's actual novel referenda finding, which is that treatment districts held (+21pp) and passed (+12pp) MORE referenda. A reader stopping at the abstract will infer that referenda failed. (c) The abstract never mentions class size, school closures, or the exploratory/appendix status of the stated-preference evidence, even though the title advertises "Voter Tax Preferences."
- "Could not commensurately counteract" and "clearly could not fully address declining appropriations" (p. 30) are asserted, never estimated. The paper never quantifies the dollar value of the passed levies against the per-pupil revenue shortfall. It is a plausible inference from two separate exhibits, not a tested claim, and the rhetoric does not signal that.
- Figure 2 is defective as published. It carries two legends that contradict each other: a top legend listing three series ("Change in TPS Enrollment vs. 2009", "Charter Schools", "Voucher Recipients") and a bottom legend listing two ("Charter Schools", "Voucher Recipients"), assigning different meanings to the same solid-circle marker. Only two series are plotted. The text on p. 9 says "in Figure 2 we thus display the contemporaneous shift in traditional public enrollment over time," but no TPS enrollment series appears. The text's "present day" figures (~5.5% charter share; 1 voucher student per 14 public students, i.e. ~7%) also cannot be recovered from the figure, whose series end at roughly .049 and .037 in 2019.
- Table 2 is not self-contained and is the paper's densest exhibit. Eleven model labels (M1-M11) span two pages and nine outcome panels, but they are defined only in ~4 pages of running prose (pp. 21-25); the table note simply says "See main text for model descriptions." Panel E is split across the p. 23/24 page break. The table also carries no indication of which column is preferred (M4, disclosed only in prose on p. 26).
- Table 1 describes a different sample from the one that identifies the estimates. The table reports N = 192 comparison and N = 95 treated (287 districts), and Table 2's 3,723 observations are consistent with roughly that count. But p. 31, fifteen pages later and inside the Conclusion, discloses that only "42 counties and 177 districts (99 comparison and 78 treatment)" actually contribute to the analyses under county-by-year fixed effects. Table 1 also never states the baseline year, and its note attributes p values to "two-sample t tests" while the text says significance is discussed for the county-adjusted differences — so a reader cannot tell which column the p value belongs to.
- "Class size" is a relabeled student-to-FTE-teacher ratio. The Data section concedes this in a parenthetical ("class size for simplicity"), but thereafter the text, Table 1, Table 2 and the Conclusion all say "class size," while Figure 6's panel is titled "Student to Teacher Ratio." A reader quoting "class sizes increased by 0.5 to 0.75 students" would be misquoting a staffing ratio; the figure's post-period values also run about 0.42 to 0.78, so the stated range understates the top and overstates the bottom.
- Multi-panel figures use inconsistent y-axis scales, defeating cross-panel eyeballing. Figure 5: -1000/500, -600/400, -600/200. Figure 7: -1000/1000, -400/200, -300/200, -500/1000. Figure 9: the econ-disadvantaged panel runs -.1/.1 while the others run -.15/.05. Nothing in the notes warns readers.
- Several load-bearing quantitative claims appear only in prose, with no exhibit and no standard errors: the housing-value DD ("median housing values decline ~2.4% in treatment districts," p. 33), the first-referendum-only analysis (8, 3, and 11 pp, p. 27), the geographic-proximity statistics (12% vs 35% within five miles; 11.27/7.54 and 3.28/1.14 average miles, p. 34), and the CES stated-preference results. The proximity passage is also internally confusing: it introduces schools "located within 5 miles" and then reports an average distance of 11.27 miles "for this group of schools."
- Notation is reused across models. Equation 1 uses gamma-T for event-study coefficients; Equation 4 uses gamma for the post-period slope shift and delta for the level shift; Note 7 uses theta both for the LEA fixed effect and for the Treat main effect; Note 8 uses gamma-s for a subject fixed effect alongside gamma-T. The text also says Time is "recentered such that data collected for the first post-treatment year of 2011 have a value of zero" while the formula given is Time = Year - 2012, and the next sentence refers to "the first school year after 2012."
- Copyediting errors survived production: "reported to be to using school choice" (p. 2); the garbled "Fleming in Milwaukee (2014), who documented that voucher parents were more likely to see the government's role in education policy" (p. 4, predicate incomplete); "Mann & Bruno, 2020" on p. 3 versus "Mann & Bruno, 2022" on pp. 4 and 5 with only a 2022 reference-list entry; and reference-list errors (Jackson, Johnson & Persico 2016 listed as "QJE, 157, 218"; Ridley & Terrier 2025 as "1356-140").
- A confound raised in the paper's own context section is never revisited. Page 10 documents that the 2008 levy-replacement grants expired in 2011 and ARRA funds lapsed in 2011 — the treatment year. The robustness section addresses the co-occurring collective-bargaining reform (M7) and the treatment-assignment covariates (M6) but never returns to the coincident fiscal cliff, which would plausibly hit larger, higher-poverty districts — precisely the treatment group — differentially.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Read the abstract as a headline, not a summary. Two of its four clauses need correcting from the body: the referenda finding is that treatment districts held and passed MORE referenda (Figure 8: +21pp held, +12pp passed, driven by capital measures), and the claim that levies "could not commensurately counteract" shrinking revenues is an inference across two exhibits, never an estimate.
- Do not quote the p. 17 sentence that post-2011 confidence intervals "do not contain zero" or that pre-2011 coefficients "contain zero." Check Figure 5 (2007 current expenditures, +258) and Figure 7 (2006 total revenue +504, local revenue +521) yourself — those pre-period CIs exclude zero. The paper's own p. 25 discussion of the -44.59 pre-trend for current expenditures is the more accurate statement.
- Before citing this paper for the claim that school choice reduces LOCAL revenues, read Table 2 Panel G across all eleven columns. The result is significant only in M1 (the simple DD), insignificant everywhere else, and positive in M2 and M3. Treat the total-revenue result (Panel D, -311.5** in the preferred M4) as the defensible finding and the local-source decomposition as suggestive.
- The most reliable finance result is total and current per-pupil expenditures: significant in M1 and M4-M8 in Table 2 Panels A and B, with a nonparametric ES pattern in Figure 5 that grows monotonically to -682 in 2019 (the text's "up to 700" and "~6.4% of baseline" both check out against Table 1's treated mean of \$10,604.65). Capital outlays are much weaker than the prose implies — "both capital and current outlays are affected" overstates Panel C, which is insignificant in the preferred M4 and in most of Figure 5's post-period years.
- For the achievement finding (Figure 9), note that only TWO pre-period points exist (2009 and 2010) because SEDA coverage starts in 2008-09. Parallel trends is barely testable here, and the non-econ-disadvantaged panel's 2009 coefficient (-.029) has a CI excluding zero. The "substantially negative" language rests on the 2019 endpoint (-.097 SD for all students, CI roughly -.15 to -.04) — the final year of the panel, with the widest interval.
- Treat "strikingly similar across subgroups" (p. 29) as approximate. Economically disadvantaged students show larger early gains (up to +.053) and a smaller terminal decline (-.067) than male students (+.033 then -.11). The shape is similar; the magnitudes differ by 40% or more, and the panels use different y-axis scales.
- Whenever the paper says "class size," read "student-to-FTE-teacher ratio." Figure 6's own panel title is the accurate label. Quote the ratio, not classroom headcount.
- Table 2 cannot be read on its own. Before opening it, read pp. 21-26 and write down what M1-M11 are; note that M4 (2009 onward, three pre-years) is the authors' preferred column, disclosed only in prose on p. 26.
- Cite the sample as 177 districts (99 comparison, 78 treatment) across 42 counties — the effective analytic sample disclosed on p. 31 — not the 287 districts in Table 1 or the ~287-district implied count behind Table 2's 3,723 observations.
- Do not read the text's Indiana context statistics off Figure 2. The figure's two legends contradict each other and the TPS enrollment series the text promises is not plotted; the "~5.5% charter" and "1 in 14 voucher" figures cannot be recovered from it.
- Sections you can skim: "Theoretical Frameworks" (pp. 5-8) is conventional policy-feedback and economies-of-scale material that does not change how you read the estimates. Sections you must not skim: "The Indiana State Context" (pp. 8-11), especially the paragraph on the 2008 circuit breaker, the 2011 expiration of levy-replacement grants, and the 2011 ARRA lapse — the paper raises these coincident fiscal shocks and never returns to them as identification threats; and the treatment-construction discussion (pp. 13-15), since "treatment" is a predicted top-tercile exposure score, not an observed policy assignment.
- Claims with no exhibit behind them, which should be cited as unverified: the -2.4% housing-value DD (p. 33), the first-referendum-only estimates of 8/3/11 pp (p. 27), the school-proximity distance statistics (p. 34, whose "11.27 miles" for schools "within 5 miles" is self-contradictory as written), and everything drawn from the CES stated-preference analysis, which lives entirely in Supplementary Appendix D and which the authors themselves label exploratory and imprecise.
- If you care about RQ4 (whether voter preferences explain the revenue effects), be aware that the main text answers it only indirectly through referenda; the stated-preference evidence the title advertises is in the online supplement, not the article.

**Detailed Commentary:**

This is a competently written, well-structured empirical paper whose exposition is let down by a recurring pattern: the prose states results more categorically than the exhibits support, and the paper's own later text often supplies the correction. The single clearest instance is on p. 17, where the Results open by asserting that post-2011 confidence intervals do not contain zero and that pre-2011 coefficients do. Both halves fail on the paper's own figures. In Figure 5's current-expenditures panel, the 2007 coefficient of +258 has a 90% interval running roughly from +55 to +465 — comfortably excluding zero. In Figure 7, the 2006 coefficients for total revenue (+504) and local revenue (+521) both sit well above zero with intervals excluding it, and the visible pre-2011 descent from +504 to near zero is exactly the kind of trajectory the parallel-trends assumption forbids. Eight pages later, on p. 25, the authors themselves write that current per-pupil spending "is going down in treatment LEAs by about 45 dollars per year, something that can be observed visually in the associated ES figure (Figure 5)." A reader who takes the Results section at face value will not know this; a reader who reaches the robustness section will. The revenue section (p. 20) is more honest, conceding a "downward pre-2011 trajectory for per-pupil revenues from all and local sources" — but it defends only by noting the differences "are not statistically significant in 2008-09 and 2009-10," which quietly steps past the significant 2005-06 coefficients.

The second structural fidelity problem concerns the local-revenue mechanism. The abstract's political-economy framing, the Conclusion's "primarily driven by fewer dollars being received through local sources," and the housing-value explanation on p. 33 all rest on the local-revenue estimate. Table 2 Panel G shows that estimate is significant in exactly one of eleven specifications — M1, the simple DD with no pre-trend adjustment (-297.1***) — and is insignificant in all ten others, positive in two of them (+178.5 in M2, +72.29 in M3), and -125.8 (141.2) in the authors' own preferred M4. Under M4 the only significant revenue result is the total (-311.5**); federal, state, and local components are each insignificant.
