The Results section is careful about this ("not consistently significant... when disentangled"); the Conclusion and abstract are not. The gap between the two matters because the local-source result is the load-bearing link in the paper's causal story from choice to weakened local tax support.

Third, the abstract itself has two defects. Its second sentence — "little rigorous work confirms the conceptual link between privatization and increased competition in K-12 education with enthusiasm for public goods and the tax policies they require" — is missing a modifier (presumably "decreased") and as printed asserts something close to the opposite of the paper's thesis. And by describing only the failure of referenda to "commensurately counteract" revenue losses, it suppresses the paper's most novel positive finding: treatment districts were 21 percentage points more likely to hold and 12 points more likely to pass a referendum (Figure 8). Both numbers check out against the figure. Note too that the paper never puts a dollar value on the passed levies, so "commensurately" is doing rhetorical work no estimate supports; a reader wanting that comparison will not find it anywhere in the article.

On exhibits: the numbers I could check between text and figures generally hold. "Up to 700 fewer dollars" corresponds to -682 (Figure 5, 2019); "~6.4% of baseline total expenditures" is exactly 682/10,604.65 using Table 1's treated mean; "up to 450 dollars per pupil" corresponds to -448 (Figure 7); "up to 4% fewer schools" corresponds to -.042 in logs (Figure 6); the 21pp and 12pp referenda figures match Figure 8. The "approximately 0.5 to 0.75 students" class-size range is slightly off (Figure 6's post-period points run about 0.42 to 0.78), and the "class size" label is itself a rename of a student-to-FTE-teacher ratio that Figure 6 correctly titles otherwise. Table 1's arithmetic is internally consistent (differences equal the mean gaps; federal + state + local revenues sum to total in both columns).

Where the exhibits fail is self-containment. Figure 2 is the worst case: two legends assign different labels to the same marker, and the TPS enrollment series the text explicitly says is displayed is not there. Table 2 is the paper's robustness centerpiece and requires the reader to carry eleven prose-defined model specifications across four pages, with no indication in the table of which column is preferred. Table 1 gives no baseline year, attributes its p values to two-sample t tests while the text says they refer to the county-adjusted column, and — most consequentially — reports 287 districts when only 177 actually contribute to the estimates, a fact disclosed for the first time on p. 31, inside the Conclusion. Figure 8 reports effects in proportions with no baseline rates shown, so a 0.21 effect is uninterpretable from the exhibit alone (the relevant base rate, that fewer than 10% of districts hold a vote in any year, is buried on p. 28). Every multi-panel figure uses different y-axis scales across panels without warning.

The paper's real expository strengths deserve equal weight. The organization is clean and predictable, the five research questions are answered in order, and the decision to interleave robustness discussion with results rather than banish it to an appendix is genuinely reader-serving. The pp. 25-26 discussion of why the nonparametric event study is preferred to the parametric linear one — including the explicit point that the linear model would have hidden the nonlinear achievement reversal — is a small pedagogical set piece. The Conclusion is a model of specific, non-defensive limitation-writing: the authors name the composition problem in SEDA, the rho ~ .75 correlation that prevents separating voucher from charter effects, the mismatch between CES's federal-spending questions and local tax attitudes, and the cross-district enrollment problem, and they surface a contradicting study (Adger & Felegi 2024) rather than burying it. The one confound the Conclusion does not revisit is the one the paper itself introduces on p. 10 — the simultaneous 2011 expiration of levy-replacement grants and ARRA funds — which a reader should hold in mind independently, since county-by-year fixed effects will not absorb shocks that scale with district size and poverty.

Bottom line for readers: this is a paper whose figures are more trustworthy than its sentences. The direction and rough magnitude of the expenditure decline and the achievement reversal are well supported and clearly presented. The revenue decomposition, the referenda-versus-revenue "insufficiency" claim, and the stated-preference evidence are all softer than the prose, the abstract, and the title suggest. Verify before quoting.

---

### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

Chin and Chen assemble an unusually complete chain of outcomes — district expenditures, revenues by source, operational inputs, local property-tax referenda, and district test achievement — for a single, well-defined policy shock (Indiana's simultaneous 2011 voucher launch and charter-authorizer expansion), estimated with a common event-study/DD design using predicted choice exposure as treatment dosage. The genuinely new pieces are the referenda-as-revealed-tax-preference outcome and the fact that the fiscal, input, and achievement links are estimated in one setting under one design; the expenditure and class-size findings largely corroborate an existing literature. The paper's contribution is real and its self-assessment is unusually candid, but its two most quotable claims — long-run negative achievement effects and districts' inability to offset revenue losses through referenda — rest on materially weaker evidence than its expenditure and class-size results.

**Strengths:**

- The voter tax-referenda outcome is a genuine addition. Almost no prior causal work connects K-12 privatization to the actual fiscal-political behavior of local electorates; the closest antecedents (Fleming 2014 in Milwaukee, Casalaspi 2019 in Michigan, Cook et al. 2020 in Ohio) are either turnout-focused or rest on weaker designs. Bringing hand-verified Indiana referendum records (CEEP data cross-checked against Secretary of State results) into a DD framework is a concrete data contribution the field can build on.
- The joint estimation of finance, inputs, and achievement in the same context under the same design is rarer than it sounds. The authors correctly identify that most of this literature estimates either fiscal spillovers or student effects, not both (Buerger & Bifulco, Mann & Bruno, and Ridley & Terrier are the named exceptions), so the paper can speak to the Figure 1 mechanism chain rather than just one link.
- Indiana's 2011 bundle is a substantively important and understudied case: the second-largest voucher program in the country by enrollment, layered onto a state that had just (2008) capped local property levies and shifted the general fund to state support. The state-specific evidence is worth having on its own terms, and the paper is right that fiscal effects of choice should be expected to be heterogeneous across finance systems rather than pooled into a single national parameter.
- The paper is honest about its boundaries in a way that improves its usefulness: it flags that vouchers and charters cannot be disentangled (predicted uptakes correlate at rho ~ .75), that the CES stated-preference evidence is exploratory and asks about Congress rather than local government, that SEDA district means cannot separate district contribution from compositional change, that class size and schools-in-operation show visual pre-trends, and that Adger and Felegi (2024) reach an opposite achievement conclusion with student-level data.
- An underrated, well-supported sub-finding: choice-exposed districts win referenda for capital projects but not for day-to-day operations. This survives the most demanding restriction the authors impose (first referendum only: 11 pp for capital and significant; 3 pp for operational and not), and it is a specific, mechanism-relevant fact about what local electorates will and will not fund under fiscal stress.

**Weaknesses:**

- The headline achievement claim is the paper's most fragile result and its most citable one. The estimand from district-mean SEDA data is "what happened to average scores in exposed districts," which mixes any true effect on remaining students with compositional drift as families exit to vouchers and charters. The subgroup cuts hold constant observable characteristics but not within-subgroup selection, and the specific short-run-positive-then-long-run-negative shape is exactly the pattern differential composition drift would generate as voucher caps lifted in 2013-14 and uptake accelerated. The paper says this plainly, but the abstract's "short-term achievement gains reversed and became substantially negative over time" will travel far past the caveat.
- Adger and Felegi (2024), using student-level data on the same state and the same voucher expansion, find that exposed traditional public schools improved. The paper notes this in a paragraph and distinguishes the two studies by scope (their design covers vouchers, not the joint charter-plus-voucher system exposure), but it does not reconcile the opposite sign or test whether its own achievement pattern survives a design closer to theirs. A reader cannot conclude from this paper that Indiana's choice expansion lowered student learning.
- The revenue-decline claim, which is load-bearing for the political-economy story, is not robust across the paper's own specifications. In Table 2 Panel D, total per-pupil revenue is significant in M1 and M4 but insignificant in M2, M3, M6, M8, M10, and M11. Local revenue (Panel G) is significant only in the simple DD (M1); in the preferred parametric specification M4 it is -125.8 (SE 141.2), and in M3 it is positive. Yet "revenue losses driven by local sources" is the empirical hook for the argument that local tax preferences weakened. Expenditures (Panels A and B) and class size (Panel H) are far more consistently signed and significant.
- The "districts could not counteract shrinking revenues through referenda" claim is an inference across two separately estimated models, not a test. Nothing in the design quantifies how much referendum revenue was raised against how much appropriation was lost; the conclusion follows from a negative revenue coefficient (itself fragile, above) sitting alongside a positive referendum coefficient. A reader who wants the offset magnitude will not find it here.
- The referenda results themselves shrink under scrutiny. The main estimates (up to 21 pp more likely to hold a vote, 12 pp to hold and pass) come from a simple pooled pre/post DD that by construction cannot show pre-trends; the event-study version yields 5 pp for holding any referendum, concentrated in capital measures, and the first-referendum-only restriction attenuates the rest to insignificance. Fewer than 10 percent (often under 5 percent) of districts hold a vote in any given year, so this is a thin-outcome setting.
- The direction of the referenda result is the opposite of the policy-feedback prediction the paper motivates — exposed districts ask for and win more tax increases — and the "weakened preferences" reading is rescued mainly by the CES stated-preference analysis, which the authors themselves say is exploratory, imprecise, asks about federal spending, and represents state adults rather than district electorates. The theoretical contribution is therefore more suggested than demonstrated.
- 2011 is a crowded treatment year in Indiana: ARRA funds lapsed, levy replacement grants from the 2008 circuit-breaker transition expired, and collective bargaining reform (including removing class size from negotiation) took effect. County-by-year fixed effects absorb shocks common within county, but treatment districts are defined by baseline demographics — far larger, far higher-FRPL, far higher share Black — so any shock whose bite scales with poverty or size loads onto the treatment coefficient. The federal revenue decline in particular is what an ARRA/Title I unwinding in high-poverty districts would look like. M6 and M7 address parts of this, and the class-size result survives M7, but the co-timing is a standing caution rather than a resolved issue.
- Because treatment is predicted exposure built from baseline proportion Black, single-mother share, and proximity to private and charter schools, "treated" is largely a label for urban, higher-poverty districts. That is a defensible dosage strategy, but it means the estimates answer "what happened to Indiana's urban, high-poverty districts after 2011 relative to co-county neighbors," and readers should carry that framing rather than a generic "districts facing competition."

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Cite it for: causal-quality evidence that Indiana districts most exposed to the 2011 choice expansion reduced per-pupil expenditures (roughly 6.4 percent of baseline total spending at the largest estimate, with current outlays consistently affected) and raised student-to-teacher ratios by about 0.5 to 0.75. These are the paper's best-supported results and survive its robustness battery.
- Cite it for: the specific and novel finding that choice-exposed districts pursue and pass property-tax referenda at higher rates, but that the effect is concentrated in capital rather than operational levies — i.e., electorates under choice pressure will fund buildings more readily than instruction. This is the paper's most distinctive policy-relevant fact and it survives the first-referendum-only restriction.
- Cite it for: the case that fiscal effects of school choice are state-specific and must be estimated separately by finance system, and as the reference point for Indiana's 2011 voucher-plus-charter-authorizer bundle.
- Do not lean on it for: "school choice lowers student achievement in public schools." The achievement outcome is a district mean from SEDA that cannot separate a causal effect on remaining students from compositional change as families exit, and student-level work on the same state and policy (Adger and Felegi 2024) reaches the opposite conclusion.
- Do not lean on it for: "school choice reduces local revenue" or "local property-tax revenue fell." The local-revenue coefficient is significant only in the simplest DD and is insignificant, and in one specification positive, across most of the paper's own robustness columns.
- Do not lean on it for: "referenda cannot offset choice-induced revenue losses." The offset is inferred by juxtaposing two separately estimated models, not measured; the paper reports no estimate of levy dollars raised against appropriations lost.
- Do not lean on it for: "school choice makes voters less willing to fund public goods." The revealed-preference result points the other way (more referenda held and passed), and the attitudinal evidence supporting the weakening-preferences reading is the exploratory CES analysis the authors explicitly caution against overinterpreting.
- Do not lean on it for: separating voucher effects from charter effects. The two policies passed in the same month and the predicted uptakes correlate at about .75; the paper is explicit that it cannot disentangle them, and the composite measure is more strongly driven by the charter component.
- Open question for readers: how much of the achievement trajectory is compositional? Resolving this requires Indiana student-level administrative records and would settle the conflict with Adger and Felegi (2024).
- Open question for readers: what mechanism actually drives the per-pupil revenue decline? The authors' preferred explanation — a roughly 2.4 percent decline in median housing values eroding the property tax base — is a plausible but supplementary DD result, and it competes with mechanical composition effects on complexity and Title I dollars and with the 2011 expiration of ARRA and levy-replacement funds.
- Open question for readers: whether the findings extend to states without Indiana's specific fiscal architecture — the 2008 circuit-breaker levy caps, referendum-gated local revenue, state-dominant general fund, and 2011 restrictions that removed class size from collective bargaining. The authors flag the bargaining constraint as a boundary on external validity themselves.

**Detailed Commentary:**

What is genuinely new here, and what is confirmation. Three things are new. First, the referenda outcome: bringing district-level property-tax referendum records into a quasi-experimental design as a measure of revealed community preference for funding public schools is, as far as the paper's own literature review and mine can tell, without close precedent in the school choice literature. Prior work on the political consequences of choice measured turnout (Cook et al. 2020; Casalaspi 2019), stated beliefs in a foreign randomized setting (Davies 2023), or interest-group polarization (Finger and Reckhow 2022). Second, the joint chain: expenditures to inputs to achievement plus the revenue-to-tax-preference loop, all estimated in one state under one design and one treatment definition. Third, Indiana's particular policy bundle, which is substantively important given the program's size. Everything else — expenditures falling under competitive pressure, class sizes rising, spending mattering for outcomes — is confirmation of a literature the paper cites accurately (Arsen and Ni; Bifulco and Reback; Cook; Ladd and Singleton; Ridley and Terrier; Jackson and Mackevicius). That confirmation still has value because it is state-specific and the paper argues persuasively that heterogeneity across finance systems is the point.

The quotability gap. The abstract advertises two claims: that districts "could not commensurately counteract shrinking revenues through local property tax referenda," and that "short-term achievement gains reversed and became substantially negative over time." Both will be quoted heavily in voucher policy debates. Neither is the paper's best-supported result. The achievement finding comes from district-average SEDA scores with no ability to follow students, in a setting where the treatment is precisely the mechanism by which district composition changes; the authors concede this and note that a student-level study of the same reform found improvements in exposed public schools. The revenue-offset claim inherits the fragility of the revenue estimates (Table 2 Panels D and G, where significance appears in only a minority of specifications and local revenue flips sign in M3) and is in any case an inference across two models rather than a measured offset. Meanwhile the results that do hold up across eleven specifications — expenditure declines and class-size increases — are less headline-friendly and will be cited less. Readers should invert the paper's rhetorical emphasis when deciding what to rely on.

The theoretical claim versus the empirical result. The paper's framing (Pierson's policy feedback; Mettler's submerged state) predicts that choice erodes support for taxing to fund public schools. The revealed-preference result runs the other way: exposed districts hold more referenda and pass more of them. The paper handles this gracefully — arguing that districts under insolvency pressure invest more effort in campaigns, that success is concentrated in capital rather than operational levies, and that residual under-funding may itself reflect weaker preferences — but the reconciliation leans on the CES stated-preference analysis that the authors themselves flag as exploratory, imprecise, aimed at federal rather than local spending, and representative of state adults rather than the relevant electorates. So the political-economy contribution is best read as opening a line of inquiry and supplying a usable outcome measure, not as establishing the feedback effect.

Identification context that bears on how far to carry the findings. Treatment is predicted exposure from an elastic-net model on baseline characteristics, and the surviving predictors — proportion Black, single-mother share, nearby private schools, in-boundary charter enrollment and counts — mean the treated group is essentially Indiana's larger, poorer, more urban, more heavily Black districts (Table 1: 6,513 versus 2,096 students; 0.11 versus 0.005 proportion Black). County-by-year fixed effects absorb shocks common within county, and M6 interacts those fixed effects with above/below median Black and single-mother shares, which is the right check. But 2011 is also the year ARRA funds and levy-replacement grants lapsed in Indiana, and those shocks bite harder in exactly the districts the model labels treated. Nothing in the paper cleanly separates a 2011 choice effect from a 2011 fiscal-cliff effect that scaled with district poverty; the federal-revenue panel is the clearest place this concern shows. I would treat the expenditure and class-size results as robust to this and the revenue decomposition as not.

Generalizability. The paper draws its boundaries honestly, and in some respects more conservatively than needed: it notes the 42 counties and 177 districts contributing to identification, notes their spread across rural, suburban, and urban settings, and explicitly warns that results may apply only to states with Indiana's collective-bargaining stipulations. Two boundaries deserve more weight than the paper gives them. Indiana's referendum-gated local revenue under the 2008 circuit breaker is unusual, and it is the institution that makes the tax-preference outcome measurable at all — which is a strength for internal logic and a limit on transfer, since most states' local revenue does not pass through discrete ballot measures. And the treatment is a bundle whose components cannot be separated, so a reader in a voucher-only or charter-only state cannot map these estimates onto their setting.

Standing in the literature. On Indiana district finance and operational inputs under the 2011 reforms, this is now the best available evidence and should become the standard citation. On the political economy of choice and local tax behavior, it is the first credible causal look and will be the reference point until better-instrumented or panel-attitudinal work arrives, with the caveat that its own result contradicts its motivating theory. On achievement, it is not the best available evidence for Indiana — student-level work is, and it points the other way. The follow-on agenda the paper sets up is clear and worth pursuing: student-level replication of the achievement path, direct measurement of the referendum revenue offset against appropriation losses, local rather than federal attitudinal data, and designs that can separate voucher from charter exposure.

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

Chin and Chen name every major data source and write out their estimating equations, fixed effects, and clustering explicitly, and nearly all of the inputs (NCES district finance/universe files, SEDA v5.0, the Private School Universe Survey, IDOE Choice Scholarship annual reports, Indiana Secretary of State election returns) are public, so the analytic dataset is in principle rebuildable from the article plus its online supplement. But there is no data availability statement beyond "Supplemental material is available online," no deposited replication package or code, no stated software environment, and several concrete construction steps — the elastic-net tuning and candidate predictor set, the price deflator, the panel's sample-inclusion rules, and the ACS-to-LEA geocoding behind the housing-value claim — are undocumented enough that an independent replication would have to guess at choices that move the headline magnitudes.

**Strengths:**

- Data sources are named individually and matched to the outcomes they supply: NCES for district expenditures (total, current, capital), revenues (federal, state, local, property tax), student-to-FTE-teacher ratio and schools in operation; IDOE for enrollment and voucher losses by district of legal settlement; SEDA v5.0 for achievement and baseline covariates; PSS 2009-10 for private school counts and proximity; IU Center for Evaluation and Education Policy plus Secretary of State returns for referenda. Nearly all are public and, unusually, the paper says the referenda data were cross-verified against a second source.
- SEDA is cited to a persistent identifier (purl.stanford.edu/cs829jn7849) with the version number (5.0) and the technical documentation (Fahle et al., 2024) — the single best-documented input in the paper, and the one on which the achievement findings rest. PSS 2009-10 and the IDOE Choice Scholarship Program Annual Reports are likewise named specifically enough that a replicator can find the exact files.
- The core specifications are written out rather than described. Equation 1 gives the nonparametric event study with LEA fixed effects, county-by-year fixed effects, event-time indicators interacted with treatment, an omitted baseline of 2010-11, and district-clustered standard errors. Equation 4 gives the parametric linear variant with its pre-trend, slope-shift, and level-shift coefficients. Note 7 writes out the simple DD used for referenda, including the deliberate choice not to condition passage on holding a referendum. Note 8 writes out the achievement model with added grade and subject fixed effects and states the weighting (number of assessments underlying each LEA-grade-subject-year mean). Weighting is stated exactly where it matters most.
- Treatment construction is documented in more detail than is typical for a machine-learning-assisted exposure measure: the CHOICERATIO outcome is defined algebraically (charter plus voucher counts over 2012-2019, averaged, scaled by baseline 2010 traditional public enrollment), the five elastic-net-retained predictors are enumerated (proportion Black, proportion single mother, private schools within 2 miles, charter enrollment, in-boundary charter school count), the second-stage adjusted R-squared (~0.73) is reported, the trichotomization rule and top-tercile treatment definition are stated, and Note 4 reports a jackknife check on predicted dosage plus a first-stage-style event study confirming the measure predicts actual choice uptake.
- Table 2 is a genuinely transparent robustness exhibit: eleven specifications across nine outcome panels, each cell reporting a coefficient, a district-clustered standard error, and an observation count, with the specification changes (pre-period length, interacted county-by-year trends, collective bargaining control, alternative treatment definitions, continuous ventile dosage, inverse propensity weighting, non-bordering comparison districts) described in the text. Group sizes are given for both the definitional sample (95 treated, 192 comparison) and the sample that actually contributes identifying variation under county-by-year fixed effects (78 treated, 99 comparison, 42 counties).
- The supplement is extensive and its contents are signposted in the main text (Appendices A through K), including tabular versions of every event study figure (Tables A1, A2), alternative treatment definitions (B), propensity weighting (C), the CES analysis (D), disaggregated expenditure categories (E), the collective bargaining reform check (K), and a nine-year-pre-period event study (Figure H1). Readers are told where each unreported result lives.

**Weaknesses:**

- No data availability statement, no replication package, no posted code, and no repository link. The Supplemental Material section reads only "Supplemental material for this article is available online." For a 2026 AERJ article built almost entirely on public data, the absence of even a lightweight code deposit is the paper's largest transparency gap — nothing here is restricted-use except the collective bargaining measure, so there is no legal obstacle to a full package.
- No software environment is reported anywhere: no language, no version, no packages. This matters most for the elastic net, where results are implementation-dependent (glmnet versus scikit-learn differ in penalty parameterization and standardization defaults).
- The elastic net that defines treatment is the least reproducible step in the paper. The candidate predictor set is described only as "all variables from the aforementioned SEDA and PSS databases collected in 2009-10" and never enumerated; the alpha and lambda values are not reported; the number of cross-validation folds is not stated; whether lambda-min or lambda-1se was used is not stated; predictor standardization is not stated; and no random seed is given, so even the same code on the same data need not reselect the same five predictors. The selected set and the second-stage R-squared are reported, which substantially mitigates this — a replicator can skip the selection step and rebuild the exposure index directly — but the selection itself cannot be reproduced or falsified.
- The NCES source files are not identified. "The National Center for Education Statistics supplies... expenditures... revenues... school operational measures" does not say F-33 / CCD School District Finance Survey versus the ELSI tabulations, does not give the release vintage, and does not say which file supplies FTE teacher counts and operational school counts (presumably the CCD LEA and school universe files). Given known revisions across F-33 vintages, a replicator would have to guess a file and a vintage.
- The price adjustment is unspecified. Finance measures are described as "inflation-adjusted" with no index (CPI-U, CPI-U-RS, GDP deflator, or an education-specific comparable wage index) and no base year. Every dollar magnitude in the paper — the ~\$700 per-pupil expenditure decline, the ~\$450 revenue decline, the -\$521 M4 coefficient, the 6.4%-of-baseline framing — is therefore not exactly reproducible; a replicator will land near but not on these numbers, with no way to tell whether a discrepancy signals a deflator difference or a real coding difference.
- Sample construction rules are never stated. There is no description of which Indiana LEAs were retained or dropped (charter LEAs, special-education cooperatives, non-operating or joint districts, districts with incomplete finance years), and no account of missingness in the unbalanced panel. The observation counts are hard to rationalize from the text: 287 districts across the 2006-2019 panel would give 3,731 district-years against a reported 3,723 (and 3,702 for the class-size panel), M4's 2009-onward sample reports 2,925 rather than the ~3,157 an 11-year balanced panel implies, and M5's 2003-onward sample reports 4,521 against ~4,879. Roughly eight to two hundred observations are dropped for reasons the paper does not explain, and the reported Ns also appear to include districts in single-treatment-status counties that cannot contribute identifying variation under county-by-year fixed effects (the text elsewhere reports only 177 contributing districts). A replicator cannot tell whether they have matched the estimation sample.
- Equation 4's time recentering is stated inconsistently: "Time_t being recentered such that data collected for the first post-treatment year of 2011 have a value of zero, that is, Time_t = Year_t - 2012," followed by the description of delta as a discontinuity "in the first school year after 2012." 2011 and 2012 cannot both be the zero point. Since delta is the single coefficient carried across all eleven robustness columns of Table 2, a replicator must choose the centering by trial and error to match the published numbers.
- Two substantive claims are reported without any uncertainty, sample size, table, or even an appendix pointer. The mechanism claim that median housing values decline ~2.4% in treatment districts is stated in the Conclusion with no standard error and no N, and the ACS-to-LEA geocoding procedure (which crosswalk, which geographies, how block-group or tract estimates were aggregated to district boundaries, how boundary changes were handled) is entirely undescribed. Similarly, the attenuated first-referendum-only results (8, 3, and 11 percentage points) are given in text with no standard errors and only a verbal significance claim. These are effectively unverifiable as reported.
- The collective bargaining agreement strength measure used in M7 came from a personal source (acknowledged to Dr. Tara Dunderdale) with no citation, no construction description in the main text, and no access pathway. The robustness check that rules out Indiana's co-occurring 2011 teacher policy reform — arguably the most important confounder in the paper — therefore cannot be independently rerun.
- The CES analysis (Appendix D), which supplies the paper's stated-preference mechanism, is characterized in the main text without survey years, waves, item wording, the geographic assignment of respondents to districts, or sample sizes; the authors note the items "suffer from more missingness" but quantify none of it. The referenda data are described as "comb[ed]" from a CEEP source with no dataset name, URL, or coding protocol for classifying operational versus capital levies — an assembled dataset that is central to the political-economy contribution and that a replicator would have to rebuild from scratch.
- Headline event-study estimates appear in the main text only as figures (Figures 5-9) with 90% confidence intervals; the point estimates and standard errors live in Supplementary Tables A1 and A2. This is signposted and acceptable, but the 90% intervals are a non-default choice that is never justified, and readers comparing these results to the conventional 95% literature will overstate the precision of the marginal findings unless they go to the supplement.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Before citing any dollar magnitude from this paper, request the deflator and base year from the authors. No inflation adjustment is named, so the per-pupil expenditure and revenue effects (~\$700, ~\$450, and the Table 2 coefficients) cannot be reproduced exactly, and the 6.4%-of-baseline framing depends on the same unstated choice.
- Treat the treatment assignment as the pivot of the whole paper and verify it first. A replicator can rebuild it without the elastic net: regress the 2012-2019 average choice ratio (charter plus voucher over baseline 2010 traditional public enrollment) on the five named predictors using SEDA 2009-10 and PSS 2009-10, check that adjusted R-squared lands near 0.73, take the linear prediction, trichotomize, and confirm the top tercile gives 95 treated and 192 comparison districts. If those counts reproduce, the rest of the paper is worth pursuing; if they do not, nothing downstream can be matched. Note that the elastic-net selection step itself is not reproducible as reported (no candidate list, no alpha or lambda, no folds, no seed, no software), so this reconstruction verifies the output, not the procedure.
- Ask the authors for the estimation sample definition and a district-year inclusion flag before attempting to match any coefficient. The observation counts in Table 2 do not follow mechanically from 287 districts times the stated year ranges (3,723 versus 3,731 for the full panel; 2,925 versus roughly 3,157 for the 2009-onward M4; 4,521 versus roughly 4,879 for the 2003-onward M5), and the text separately reports only 177 districts in 42 counties contributing identifying variation under county-by-year fixed effects. Whether the singleton-county districts sit inside the reported Ns changes what the estimates are averaging over.
- Pin down which NCES files were used. Request the specific survey and vintage for expenditures and revenues (F-33 / CCD School District Finance Survey, and which release year) and for FTE teachers and operational school counts. F-33 revisions across vintages are large enough to shift district-level per-pupil figures, and the paper's description does not identify the extract.
- When rerunning Equation 4, resolve the time-centering contradiction empirically. The text says the zero point is 2011 in one clause and Year minus 2012 in the next; try both and keep whichever reproduces the Table 2 M4 coefficients. Until that is settled, do not read the delta coefficients as anchored to a specific year.
- Do not lean on the housing-value mechanism as reported. The ~2.4% decline in median home values is given with no standard error, no sample size, no table, and no description of how ACS 2006-2010 and 2012-2016 five-year estimates were geocoded to LEA boundaries. It is the paper's stated explanation for the local revenue decline, and as printed it is unverifiable. Ask for the crosswalk and the estimation table before treating it as evidence rather than conjecture.
- Treat the CES stated-preference results (Appendix D) as the least verifiable claim in the paper and read the authors' own caveats as binding. The main text gives no waves, item wording, respondent-to-district assignment rule, or Ns, and the authors themselves flag imprecision, item missingness, and the mismatch between federal-spending questions and local district outcomes. This is the mechanism link between the revenue findings and the political-economy framing, and it is the piece a reader should hold most loosely.
- Read the tabular supplement, not the figures, before drawing inferences about marginal effects. Figures 5-9 use 90% confidence intervals, so several findings that appear to exclude zero would not at conventional 95% levels; Supplementary Tables A1 and A2 carry the point estimates and standard errors. The class-size and schools-in-operation results in particular warrant this check, since the authors acknowledge visible pre-trends in both.
- Recognize that the M7 collective bargaining robustness check cannot be independently reproduced — the measure came from a private source with no citation or access pathway. Since Indiana's 2011 collective bargaining restrictions are the most direct alternative explanation for expenditure cuts and class-size increases (the authors themselves note unions could no longer negotiate over class size after 2011), a reader who wants this confounder ruled out must request the data or reconstruct a bargaining-strength measure independently.
- Ask whether a replication package can be deposited. Essentially every input except the collective bargaining measure is public, so there is no confidentiality barrier to posting the analysis code, the assembled referenda dataset, the elastic-net script with its seed, and the ACS-to-LEA crosswalk. Absent that, the finance and achievement results are approximately reproducible with effort, while the referenda-coding, housing-value, and CES results are not.

**Detailed Commentary:**

The right way to read this paper's reproducibility is to separate three tiers of claims, because they are verifiable to very different degrees.

The first tier — the district finance, class size, schools-in-operation, and SEDA achievement results — is close to reproducible from public data. The sources are the standard NCES district finance and universe files, IDOE enrollment and Choice Scholarship annual reports, and SEDA v5.0, which is cited to a persistent Stanford handle with a version number and technical documentation. Equations 1 and 4 and Notes 7 and 8 write out the fixed effects (LEA plus county-by-year; grade and subject added for achievement), the omitted baseline (2010-11), the clustering (district), and the weighting (assessment counts for achievement, unstated and presumably absent elsewhere). Table 2 reports coefficients, standard errors, and Ns across eleven specifications. A determined replicator with the public files would get to something recognizably close to Figures 5 through 7 and Table 2. What would stop an exact match are three unstated choices: the deflator and base year, the sample-inclusion rules, and the Equation 4 time centering. None is exotic, and all three are the kind of thing a two-page supplement or a code deposit would settle.

The second tier is the treatment variable, which is a special case because it is machine-learning-generated. As reported, the elastic-net step is not reproducible — the candidate predictor set is described only as everything in SEDA and PSS for 2009-10 and is never enumerated, and no alpha, lambda, fold count, standardization convention, seed, or software is given. But the authors do something that substantially rescues this: they name all five retained predictors, report the second-stage adjusted R-squared (~0.73), state the trichotomization rule, report the resulting group sizes, note a jackknife stability check, and show in Note 4 and Appendix Figure A2 that the predicted dosage significantly predicts realized choice uptake after 2011. That means a replicator can bypass the irreproducible step entirely and rebuild the exposure index from the five named variables, then check the 95/192 split. This is why the paper lands at adequate rather than weak: the pipeline has an unreproducible link, but the authors documented the link's output well enough to reconstruct around it. Readers should still register that the researcher-degrees-of-freedom argument the authors advance for using the elastic net — that it removes their own judgment from predictor selection — is only as strong as the tuning choices they do not report, since lambda selection and the candidate set are themselves discretionary.

The third tier is where verification genuinely fails, and readers should weight these claims accordingly. The referenda outcomes are a hand-assembled dataset, described as combed from an Indiana University CEEP source and verified against Secretary of State returns, with no dataset name, no URL, and no coding protocol for the operational-versus-capital distinction that carries the paper's most interesting result (referenda pass more in treated districts, but mainly capital ones). The CES stated-preference analysis is characterized without waves, item wording, respondent-to-district assignment, or sample sizes, and the authors themselves flag imprecision and missingness — appropriately, since it is doing heavy interpretive work as the mechanism connecting the revenue decline to the political-economy story. The ACS housing-value result is the starkest case: a specific number (~2.4%) offered as the paper's preferred explanation for declining local revenues, printed in the Conclusion with no standard error, no N, no table, no appendix pointer, and no description of how five-year ACS estimates were geocoded to school district boundaries. The first-referendum-only estimates (8, 3, 11 percentage points) are similarly text-only. And the collective bargaining measure behind the M7 robustness check came from a private source with no citation, which is unfortunate given that Indiana's 2011 bargaining restrictions — which the authors acknowledge removed class size from the bargaining table in exactly the post period where they find class sizes rising — are the sharpest competing explanation for the operational-inputs findings.

On journal-era norms: this is a 2026 AERJ article with no data availability statement (the Supplemental Material section says only that supplemental material exists), no replication package, no code, and no software environment. The supplement is substantial and well-signposted across Appendices A through K, and it does carry the tabular versions of every event-study figure, so results reporting is better than the main text alone suggests. But documentation in a PDF appendix is not a replication package, and the near-complete public availability of these inputs means there was no confidentiality reason not to deposit one. A reader should conclude that the finance and achievement findings are plausibly checkable by anyone willing to spend a few weeks and make several judgment calls, that the treatment measure is reconstructible but its construction procedure is not auditable, and that the referenda-coding, tax-preference, and housing-value components — which happen to carry the paper's most novel contribution — rest substantially on trust.
